plan.title: Entropy: Why Messes Happen by Themselves
plan.description: Entropy explains why hot coffee cools, ice melts and rooms get messy. This one-minute explainer shows that it is really about how many ways things can be arranged.

beats.narration: Why does a hot coffee always cool down, but never heats itself back up? Why does a tidy room get messy, but never tidies itself? The answer is a idea called entropy.
Entropy is not just disorder. It counts the ways something can be arranged. Think of a deck of cards. Only one order is perfectly sorted, but countless orders look shuffled.

props.definition: A measure of how many ways the parts of a system can be arranged without changing how it looks overall.
props.example: A sorted deck versus a shuffled deck

beats.narration: Nature drifts toward the arrangements that are most likely. Heat spreads out. Ice melts into water. Milk mixes into tea. Each step moves from few possible arrangements to many.
This is why time seems to have a direction. The second law of thermodynamics says that in a closed system, entropy tends to rise. Order is possible, but it costs energy.
So entropy is really a story about probability. Messy states are not forced on us. There are simply far more of them. Remember that, and you will see entropy everywhere.

props.text: Messy is not forced. It is just far more likely.
